Hello, everyone, and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Red Eye.
I'm your host, Eddie Palmyan, and with me here in the studio is my friend and colleague, Niklas Savos.
How are you?
I'm happy, as we today are going to speak to Carter Johnson, the founder and manager of MCJ Capital Partners.
We met Carter in Omaha, actually, over dinner earlier this year, and realized we have a common interest in serial acquire companies.
We definitely have, and for today's episode, our guest has selected the book, Distant Force,
a memoir of the Teledyne corporation,
and the man who created it, written by Dr. George A. Robert and published in 2007.
Here comes our conversation with Carter Johnson.
Welcome to the podcast, Carter, and thank you for taking the time.
Hey, thanks for having me. Glad to be here.
And where are you today?
I'm in Denver, Colorado. So, you know, it's November when we're recording this,
we're getting to those points where we're starting to get a few snow flurries out here.
Nice. And let's start with your passion.
investing how did it begin? Yeah, so I caught the bug early on. I was always, you know, starting
these little businesses and side hustles. And when I was 12, I took some money I made from a little
long company I had and I opened up a brokerage account and my stepdad's name. And I was, I was kind of
off and running and just, you know, learning on my own and having fun and in the process.
And today I've chosen the book, Distant Force.
why is that? Yeah, so for me, when I analyze companies, I spend a lot of time on the qualitative
analysis components of it. And, you know, I really love serial acquires. So diving into distant
force and studying the internal workings and one of the best serial acquires out there, for me, that was

And some people of our listeners are, of course,
familiar with Teledyne, but some are not. And in the book, the company is described as one of the
most outstanding corporate success stories in the history of American business. So how much value did shareholders
in Teledyne gain during Henry Singleton's time at the helm? Yeah. So Simulton started the company
in 1960, went public in 1961. And you can certainly cherry-pick a few different decades,
where returns were better than others. But throughout his reign, he generated, he generated,
a 20.4 Kager for shareholders. So quite impressive, for sure.
Yeah, pretty amazing. And his right-hand man for a lot of that time was Dr. George A. Roberts, the author
of this book that we're speaking about today. Can you briefly tell us about his role and about him?
Yeah, so Dr. Dr. George Roberts, he's another fascinating guy. Him and Henry Singleton, they were
actually roommates at the U.S. Naval Academy. So they knew each other from their time in college.
Roberts started his career at a company called Basco, did really well there, rose to the ranks of
president. And then in mid-60s, about six years after Teledyne was founded, him and Henry
Singleton negotiated a merger between the two companies. And that brought Dr. George Roberts
on board. What I love about Roberts actually writing this book, you know,
we can get into some critiques and everything, but what I really love is he was very much a boots on the ground
guy within the Teledyne operation. So when they were looking at acquisitions, a lot of times he was
going out to these facilities, meeting with management, technical staff, really learning about
the business, what it needed, how it worked. So he had a really, you know, intuitive
to feel for the internal operations. And that was my goal when reading this book was really
to understand those internal workings. Eventually, after Henry Singleton retired, Dr. George Roberts
took over as the president. Eventually, he retained the position of chairman of the board until he retired.
So super knowledgeable regarding the entire company. And he gives a great first-hand account
of how a lot of things worked. And a few words maybe about the businesses that Teledyne
had? What kind of industries were they in and so on? Yeah, so regarding industries,
you know, they were very technically heavy. And we can get into that a little bit with, you know,
regards to the type of businesses. But they, especially in those years in the 60s, they were heavily
focused on acquisitions of technical companies that would create strategic advantages going
after government and military contracts. And we can talk a little bit more about Henry
about Henry Singleton's strategy with acquisitions. But that's, you know, if you're looking at a broad
stroke of the companies that Teledine largely acquired, it was these niche technical expertise. And then
the genius of Henry Singleton was he knew how to stitch these things together to create those
one plus one equals three type of situations. And some of you listeners might remember
the name Singleton from Will Thorndyke's great book, The Outsiders, which we discussed with him in episode
30. But distant force, it goes even deeper and tells more about Henry Singleton as a person. So who was he?
Yeah. Well, I think a lot of people know him as a great capital allocator. A lot of people
know that he was, you know, you know, a chess master. I love to study kind of just the
habits of high performers in general and really peel back the layers and kind of learn
more about him. A few observations regarding Henry Singleton, one, the guy was actually a health nut
and he was ahead of his time. You know, he operated it during a period where everybody was just
like smoking cigarettes nonstop in the U.S. And he was really, he was health conscious to the point where
he was, he installed, you know, a corporate gym before that was a thing, right?
Like, nobody was doing that.
He would work at a drafting table, so he would be able to, you know, stand up and just get more movement
during the day. So that's, I thought that was pretty cool, his devotion to health.
The other thing, he was also a huge computer guy. And this was before computers were
a main component in the workday. And he was always tinkering on a computer guy. And he was always tinkering
on a computer, always trying to figure the newest thing regarding computers out. And he used

component, though, about Henry Singleton. So most people know him, you know, Fort Heledine and as a serial
acquirer, fewer people know that he was a huge acquireer of he was a huge acquirer of land in the United
States, especially in the latter part of his life. He went on a spree where he was just acquiring
all these ranches across the western part of the United States. And at the time of this death,
he was actually the third largest U.S. land owner, which is pretty amazing to think. But what I find
find really fascinating is one of the things that Henry Singleton would do, he would acquire these
ranches. And then he would essentially take over the function of being
the bookkeeper. So he oversaw all the expenses. He signed all the checks. And he saw this as a form of
discipline, but he also saw it as a way to intuitively understand the operations of the actual business,
of the ranch. And I just think that's such a powerful lesson and something that we can
replicate as investors. You know, I find it really beneficial a lot of times to recreate financials
of a company by hand versus just dumping it into an Excel sheet. You pick up on those
components that, you know, doing it the hard laborous way, you just you pick up on a little bit more than

that about Singleton. And when Henry Singleton died in 1999, George Roberts, the author,
he said at the funeral that Henry was much more than a salesman, mathematician, engineer,
inventor and chess champion. He was a student. And is that something that you feel like many
of these great leaders have been during during their time? They have been a student and always wanted
to learn. Oh, that's absolutely. I think that's a constant, you know, and it's not just with the great
investors, it's also the great operators. Sam Walton comes to mind immediately. He was the same
way. He was always learning. And he would go out to the field and look at competitors and understand
and what it was that they were doing.
Obviously, Buffett and Munger talk about the values of being a lifelong learner.
And it's, yeah, that's such a constant in terms of these high performers.
They're just, they're really, they enjoy that process of learning.
So if we dig a bit deeper into Toledon, as you said, it was a serial acquirer who bought
bought actually 130 companies in eight years between 1961 and 1969.
but then actually stopped since prices had run up and also that the best companies had been bought.
Can you describe how Teledyne thought about acquisitions and what hurdle rate they used and so on?
Yeah, so, I mean, if you if you look at the early, early days, we'll start at the very beginning,
most of the first moves that Singleton made, they were geared towards more asset-based acquisitions.
And in particular, Henry Singleton focused on acquisitions that had excess capacity.
So he went out and, you know, he would buy a company that had a manufacturing plant that had a warehouse, that had labor.
And once he had that in place, he had everything he needed to then go and bid on these government contracts.
And that was, you know, that was a huge, almost like, arbitrage of resources, if you will, he knew how to do that.
once he had that in place, again, you know, Singleton, he's, he's a chess master.
So he understood how to move the pieces. And you really see that unfold with kind of his next wave
wave of acquisitions, because this is where he would focus on that, that one plus one equals three in the sense that
he would go out and he would look at companies, figure out what technology his current holdings had,
and then what technology and components he could go out and acquire and make his position
that much more competitive going after these government contracts.
So it was really, you know, he had that foresight to actually understand the process of bidding on these
government military contracts, but then also how to make them that much more competitive in that
bit process.
Once he kind of had that stabilized, he then started moving.
both upstream and downstream, acquiring manufacturers of these internal components
that would go into the end products of Teledyne.
So we really had, you know, vision just across the field, understanding where to capture value
in that value chain.
As, you know, as the entity swelled larger and larger, you really notice that Singleton focused more
more on the profitability side of acquisitions and the diversification.
He saw diversification as a way to minimize
over overall risk.
So, you know, you really start seeing the acquisitions kind of balloon out, expand out into other areas.
Regarding hurdle rates, you know, one of the things I found interesting is studying Teladine.
internally, one of the things they would mandate is a 20% hurdle rate return on assets
for their profit centers.
And any cash that profit centers, you know, retained as opposed to returning to headquarters,
that they were required to produce that 20% hurdle rate.
So I think headquarters hurdle rate was a little bit different, but that kind of gives you a good
sense of what Singleton was thinking internally in terms of returns that you've
who's trying to generate on capital.
And at Red Eye, we have this Red Eye rating where we use, we have three different categories that our
analysts use when they analyze companies.
And one is financials and one is business.
And we talk a lot about this here.
But the first one that we have is people.
And Henry Singleton actually said that people were the most important factor in a business.
So can you talk a bit about how he managed the culture while growing so quickly with
M&A?
Yeah.
Well, I think one of the advantages he has was,
much of it was decentralized, right? So Singleton was a huge believer of if your people are hitting
their marks, let them run their own show, you know, let them do their own thing. And that type of autonomy,
I think, was really valued, as it is today, but really valued during that time period.
The other thing that I think Henry Singleton did a phenomenal job of is he knew how to make people
feel important. And if you look at the
organization structure and if you look at these these profit centers, the manager of those profit centers, they would actually retain the title of president. And Singleton did this intentionally so that there was this level of credibility and respect that those individuals would garnish in their, in their community. And he encouraged them to, you know, you know, maintain those local relationships.

profit centers every year. So again, he was just, you know, bringing, bringing these

differences between some acquirers who do more of the Buffett approach, I would say,
just buy good companies and leave them. Others have a more like industrial logic behind buying
companies, and it's clear that Singleton is in that bucket, I think. And, I mean, he, I think,
my impression is that they actually bought good companies that were not really connected
connected to that if they found them, but that was not the key business.
And I mean, it seems like he early saw certain trends in the market in terms of semiconductors

And when you look at serial acquires, how, how you feel that they differ and why and so on, and when
maybe one way is better than the other, so to speak.
Yeah. So, well, I think one of the advantages Singleton had was he understood the backdrop
up going into the 60s. He understood that World War II had created this catalyst for all these new
technologies across American manufacturers, and a lot of these owners were looking to either retire
or, you know, take on capital to grow. And Singleton knew he had that environment, and, and eventually that
became, you know, so saturated that that opportunity set disappeared. We can talk a little bit
about that and how the 70s unfolded. But again, he had this backdrop. He understood the surplus of these

that one plus one equals three. He understood how to stitch these industrial manufacturers of these
technology components together to create this added gain. And I think that was, you know,
really, really advantageous, especially in the early years when they were securing these government
and military contracts.
I think nowadays, if you look at some of the best serial acquires, you know, I love following zero acquires that
really focus on acquiring these monopolistic players in these super niche markets.
And a lot of times, those have less expectations of integration and creating those one plus one
equals three situations, but, you know, they'll maintain that market share. There's a lot more
more durability there. And I would almost argue under that model, there's a little bit longer of a runway
runway, because you can keep finding these niches as opposed to being dependent on creating those
value ads with synergies of stitching multiple companies together. So those would be my
thoughts at least on that.
I mean, just just thinking about it as an investor, I can just imagine how difficult it must have been to,
as an investor to hold on to this stock when, I mean, first, they bought all these companies
and the whole playbook was, was around growing through acquisitions, and then it just
just flipped. And I mean, yeah, it definitely worked as, as we will hear more about.
But yeah, it's...
Well, and to your point, you think about it's...
it's the 60s, that was the Go-Go era. Conglomerates were the, you know, they were the
fat, they were the technology companies of this most recent bull market. So to differentiate between
Teledyne and these other conglomerates, I mean, you really had to think that you had something special
with Henry Singleton. And to your point, it would have been pretty difficult, I think, to hold on,
especially once you hear that Singleton and Roberts are shutting down this acquisition machine
that over the decade has produced these tremendous returns.
And at that moment, they also did something else inspired by General Motors,
a book that he has read Singleton, then he diversified into insurance and financial operations
because he wanted to ensure financing in these tough times that he was thinking coming.
But who would have guessed that would turn out so well?
Right, right.
It wasn't the easiest transition either. You know, there were, there were some
mishaps there. They took on some insurance that had a lot more long tail risk than what they realized
and ended up having to, to take a hit there. But yeah, I think, again, that's one of the things,
and I think what makes Henry Singleton so impressive in terms of a capital allocator.
He knew how to work both sides of the balance sheet. He knew how to work both sides of the balance sheet. He knew
how to find value in whatever it was he was doing, and he was adaptable.
So he didn't, you know, he just didn't have one lever in terms of, hey, we're just going to do acquisitions.
You know, we can talk about it, how he bought back stocks. He issued dividends. He, you know, did some creative

And if we go deeper into the fact that, as you stated, that 1 plus 1 equals 3, a lot about this is about

with managing the business units, can you tell us a bit about the methods Teledyne used?
Yeah, that to me was the most important.
And that's really what I enjoy digging into.
So, first off, when, you know, Teledyme was acquiring companies, a lot of times they would pursue
acquisitions where the owner was looking for retirement. So they were, they were going to leave the business.
And this fit well for Teledyne. They would actually go in, they would do an acquisition.
And then they would place a corporate accountant to initially take over management.
And what this would do is, they would actually go in, they would do an acquisition.
is this would create and allow a time period where they could create this uniform financial and reporting standard.

So it just makes all this much more impressive.
But if you look at the system they had for managing these entities, all of the profit centers, they had had a comptroller

And all of all the banking was local.
You know, again, single team was big on maintaining those local relationships.

a conglomerates were all the rage, but there was a lot of bloating internally and layers upon layers

that I think was unique in the teladine really tried to minimize those layers. That

as well. But I just, I mean, it's, it's different in different businesses, and it's just

populate that talk about a situation.

thesis: The speakers discuss Carter Johnson's investment philosophy centered on qualitative analysis and serial acquisition, using the memoir 'Distant Force' about Teledyne Corporation as a case study. They detail how founder Henry Singleton generated a 20.4% annual return for shareholders through niche technical acquisitions and strategic integration, while his right-hand man, Dr. George Roberts, provided first-hand insights into the company's internal operations. The conversation highlights Singleton's unique habits, such as installing a corporate gym, tinkering with early computers, and personally managing ranch bookkeeping to understand business operations, which the speakers suggest are replicable lessons for investors.
